name: Apache ORC
summary: A columnar file format born in Hive: typed columns in large stripes, built-in indexes every 10,000 rows, and the storage behind Hive’s ACID tables.
intro: An ORC file starts with the bytes `ORC`, then a body of stripes, then a tail. Each stripe holds whole rows, about 64 MB of them by default in the Java writer, and is self-contained: an index section, the row data with every column stored separately, and a stripe footer. Writers pick encodings by type (dictionary, run-length, bit packing, delta) and then compress with ZLIB, Snappy, LZ4 or ZSTD, which the Java writer now uses by default. The tail holds the schema, the list of stripes and statistics for every column, in Protocol Buffers so new fields don’t break old readers, plus a small uncompressed postscript that says how to read the rest. A reader fetches the last 16 KB of the file first and works backwards.

Indexes sit at three levels: the whole file, each stripe, and each group of 10,000 rows inside a stripe. They record counts, nulls, minimum and maximum, and sums for numbers, and columns can add bloom filters. An engine turns a filter such as `age > 100` into a search argument and skips files, stripes and row groups that can’t match. Hive builds ACID tables on ORC: updates and deletes go into delta directories of ORC files with extra columns (operation, original transaction, bucket, row id), and compactions merge them into new base files. ORC started in Hive in 2013 and became a top-level Apache project in 2015; it’s free under Apache 2.0, with Java and C++ libraries, and 2.3.1 (July 2026) is the current release.
strengths: Indexes per file, stripe and 10,000-row group, plus optional bloom filters, let engines skip most of a file on selective queries
A full set of typed columns, including decimal, `union` and two timestamp types, with the schema stored in the file
The format behind Hive’s full ACID tables (`UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `MERGE`) and streaming ingest
Column-level encryption in the format, supported by Spark since 3.2
The default format for new tables in the Hive connectors of Trino and Presto
limits: A smaller ecosystem than Parquet: Iceberg and Spark default to Parquet, and Delta Lake stores only Parquet
Files are written once; Hive’s updates pile up delta files that need compaction, and ACID is built for millions of rows per transaction, not millions of transactions an hour
ACID tables are a Hive feature, not part of the format, so other engines have to implement Hive’s transaction rules to read them correctly
Some engines only read it: Impala can query ORC tables but can’t write them
Two timestamp types: plain `timestamp` has no time zone and shows the same wall-clock time everywhere, so ORC’s docs recommend `timestamp with local time zone` unless everything is in UTC

snippet.title: A Hive ACID table on ORC, with ZSTD and a bloom filter
source: -- Hive: transactions need the DbTxnManager and concurrency support
-- written as a delta directory; compaction later folds it into the base
UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE order_id = 1;
-- stripes and 10,000-row groups whose stats or bloom filter rule out 42 are skipped
SELECT order_id, status FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;

sections.title: ORC or Parquet?
sections.intro: Both are open columnar formats from early 2013 with similar ideas: columns stored apart, statistics in a footer, files written once. The differences are in the details and, above all, in who supports them.

Min and max per column chunk; optional page index and bloom filters

story: For several years RCFile, a hybrid columnar format developed at Facebook, had been the standard way to store Hive tables on Hadoop. It kept each column value as an untyped binary blob. That meant whole values had to be read and decoded, filters couldn’t be pushed down to the file, and the file didn’t even know its row types. In January, Hortonworks co-founder Owen O’Malley opened HIVE-3874 to create an Optimized Row Columnar format, working with Facebook as part of Hortonworks’ Stinger initiative to make Hive up to 100 times faster.

ORC shipped in Hive 0.11 in May 2013, and the v1 file format still in use arrived with Hive 0.12 that October. Facebook ran its own ORC writer and reported in 2014 that switching tens of petabytes from RCFile raised compression from 5x to 8x. Hive 0.14 added ACID updates, implemented only for ORC. In April 2015 ORC became its own top-level Apache project. ORC 1.0 followed in January 2016, and from 1.1 Hadoop jobs could use ORC without pulling in Hive’s execution jar.

choices.choice: Keep the column types in the file
choices.why: RCFile stored blobs, so it couldn’t use type-specific compression or evaluate filters. ORC writes with type-aware encoders (dictionary, bit packing, delta, run-length) and stores the schema.
Minimum and maximum values for each column in each group of rows let Hive’s pushed-down filters skip whole groups without reading them.

choices.choice: Tail at the end, metadata in Protocol Buffers
choices.why: HDFS files can’t be changed after they’re written, so the top-level index goes last. Protocol Buffers let later versions add fields without breaking older readers.
Each stripe can be read with only its own bytes plus the file tail, which makes stripes the natural unit of work for distributed tasks.
